intro.text: This is Jammu and Kashmir, right up at the top of India. In the middle of it lies a wide flat valley with mountains standing all the way round it, and a river called the Jhelum winding along the bottom. Ladakh is next door. Srinagar is the main city, and it sits on a lake.

animal.text: The markhor is a wild goat living on the cliffs here. His horns spiral up like two twisted candles, longer than you are tall. He stands on his back legs to reach leaves.

food.text: Kashmir grows saffron. Every purple flower has three red threads in it, pulled out by hand, one flower at a time. About a hundred and fifty flowers make one gram.

festival.text: Lohri comes in January, on one of the coldest nights, and means the days will start getting longer. People light a bonfire and throw popcorn and peanuts into it.

hello.text: Kashmiri goes the other way on the page. You start at the right-hand edge and read towards the left, so the last letter comes first. Hello here is Namaskar.

line.text: People live on this lake in wooden houses that float, tied up in rows. To go anywhere you sit in a long thin boat and somebody paddles you there, the way you would walk down a street. There are gardens floating on the water too, growing things to sell.

A little cabin hangs from a wire and carries you up the mountain, over the snow and over the tops of the fir trees. It sets off two and a half thousand metres up and stops at nearly four thousand. Under your feet, all the way, there is nothing but air.

landmarks.name: The Tulip Garden, Srinagar
landmarks.photoQuery: Indira Gandhi Memorial Tulip Garden Srinagar

line.text: This garden was planted with more than a million and a half tulip bulbs. In spring they come up in long stripes of one colour at a time: a stripe of red, then a stripe of yellow, running away from you further than a street is long.

landmarks.name: Dachigam National Park
landmarks.photoQuery: hangul Kashmir stag Dachigam National Park

line.text: These deer are called hangul, and nearly every hangul left alive is in this one park. Twenty years ago there were fewer than two hundred of them. Now there are a bit over three hundred. A stag can carry antlers with sixteen points on them.

This fort stands on a wooded hill above a river, built of sandstone, with fat round towers along the top of its wall. The story goes that a king saw a tiger and a goat drinking from that river side by side, and neither hurt the other, so he built his city right here.
